narrative:
The model predicted an 88% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven first by your class rank at the end of your third year, which placed you in the bottom decile of your school. This was the single strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class rank, also in the bottom decile, added further weight in the same direction. Together, these two academic standing measures told the model you had struggled consistently relative to your classmates, where accepted students on average ranked near the middle of their classes.

Your LSAT score of 23, well below the average of 37 among accepted applicants, was the third most important factor and also increased the predicted risk of failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70 (versus an accepted average of 3.23), middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the overall outlook.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and a solid test score in a future application would directly address the factors that led to this rejection.
